en: Preface to the *Jichengji* (Record of the Compilation of the *Huayan Yisheng Jiaoyi Fenqizhang*) The *Appended Statements* (*Xici*) of the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*) says: "The contraction of the inchworm is for the sake of seeking extension; the hibernation of the dragon and snake is for the sake of preserving the body;
the refinement of meaning until it enters the divine is for the sake of achieving practical application. Therefore, our Vairocana Tathāgata, following the ocean...
Its seal shines forth; Jñānaprabha and Jinshān spoke with particularity, naming it the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra of the Buddha*.

The Tang National Preceptor, the Venerable Xianshou, entered through its gate and composed the *Yicheng jiaoyi fenqi* (The Delimitation of the Doctrinal Meanings of the One Vehicle) to instruct those who had not yet awakened.
Although there are many commentaries and exegeses, none have reached its source. Therefore, Master Fazhen sighed: "Alas!"
With the advent of the Xuanzhang and Zhenguan eras, the profound mysteries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the grand systems of the sutras and śāstras were nearly submerged and lost.

He felt shame that the legacy of Xianshou had perished without renown throughout his lifetime; yet, though he desired to recount his own realizations, his great vow remained unfulfilled when he suddenly passed away.

Ji [the Master] survived only as ashes from the burning of his firewood. His own responses to the *Tongjiao ce* (Exhortations on the Common Teaching), the *Xinjing lianzhu ji* (Record of the Pearl-String Commentary on the Heart Sutra), and other works circulated widely in the world, thereby providing a model for the doctrinal studies of the Huayan school.
I, Xi Di, being unworthy, have presumptuously composed this text, all of which is based upon...

I have taken the Great Master’s teachings on the essential points of the doctrine as my primary intent. While I have also occasionally employed the explanations and specific illustrations found in previous commentaries to clarify the text, the purport of the *Jiaozhang* (Chapter on the Teachings) has thus become clear and expansive.
It is my hope that those who preach and listen will not lose themselves in a multitude of divergent paths, thereby failing to find the Way.
Mencius said, "This is what is meant by Confucius 'achieving the great synthesis. To achieve the great synthesis means to begin with the resonance of metal and conclude with the vibration of jade.
Therefore, his record is titled 'The Achievement of Synthesis.'"
On the first day of the second month in the year of Wuyin during the Jiading era of the Great Song,

(Xidi) respectfully records this preface for the first fascicle of the *Jicheng ji* (Record of the Compilation of the Chapter on the Classification of the Teachings and Meanings of the One Vehicle of the Avataṃsaka).
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Xidi, resident at Huilin Monastery in Wulin.

This brief commentary on the chapter is divided into three parts. First is the title that clarifies the essential meaning. *Avataṃsaka* refers to the scripture upon which this is based; this is fully explained in the original commentary (*Ben-shu*).
As for the term "One Vehicle" (*Ekayāna*), Xianshou said: "One" means the sense of being without another, and "Vehicle" (*yāna*) means the sense of transporting or carrying across.
Guishan said: "To comprehensively encompass without distinction is called 'One' (Ekayāna). To transport and contain all is called a 'Vehicle' (Yāna).

Therefore, it is named the One Vehicle, which is precisely the Single Buddha Vehicle. Teaching, principle, practice, and fruit are collectively termed a 'vehicle,' for they all possess the meaning of transporting [beings to liberation]."
Furthermore, one is not merely one; that is to say, all is one, and one is all. All things are not all, and one is also not one.

All phenomena interpenetrate one another; in every particular there is no obstruction. They mutually enter and mutually identify, fusing together without exception within the single Dharma-realm, for all are like illusions. Thus, the Great Sutra says: "One is many, and many..."
That is, they are equal. All dharmas in their entirety are the One Vehicle. Regarding the meaning of the teaching, Kōdō says:

"Compared to other commentaries and sub-commentaries, these are merely what is illustrated, as well as the definitions of their respective scopes; all shall be explained below. However, this title has two aspects: the subject and the object.

First, the chapters are the subject that explains, while everything above is the object being explained. Second, 'Avataṃsaka' is the expressive designation, followed by the six characters [of the title]."

Regarding the title: it is established by moving from the expression toward the intended meaning (*artha*). It adopts the name of another work in its entirety; this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound known as a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) analysis.

Within the biography of Cui Zhiyuan, one version is titled *Huayan wujiao zhang* (A Chapter on the Five Teachings of the Avataṃsaka), while another is titled *Huayan yisheng fenjiao ji* (A Record of the Divisions of the One Vehicle Teaching of the Avataṃsaka).
The author has briefly cited these for the time being.

Regarding the two honorary titles of the National Preceptors (*Guoshi*): "Jing" means "great," referring collectively to the location, namely the Western Capital of the Great Tang, which was ancient Chang'an and is now Yongxing.
"Great Jianfu Monastery" refers specifically to the particular site where [the preceptor] resided.
This excludes places such as those where one resides for state affairs or receives imperial favor. In Sanskrit it is called *vihāra*; correctly, it is *viharana*. This means "place of practice.

It is the place where ordained practitioners dwell and reside. As for the current term "temple" (*si*), since the time of Kāśyapa Mātanga’s initial arrival in the land of Han, he temporarily stayed at Honglu together with other guests.
Later, a *saṃghārāma* was constructed and named Baima (White Horse), from which the term "temple" (*si*) was derived.
Regarding the term "śramaṇa" and so forth: this specifically names the person who can expound [the teaching]. "Śramaṇa" is a Sanskrit term;
its full form is *śramaṇa*, which translates here as "diligent in cessation. Thus, a sutra says: "One who has stilled the mind and reached the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa.

However, there are distinctions between the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), as well as between the path of demonstration and the path of practice, as in the *Daśacakra-sūtra*. The following two characters refer to the Teacher.

This is his name. Both his courtesy name and his title are Xianshou (Worthy Head). He was born during the Tang dynasty and served as the teacher to the Golden Wheel Emperor, as detailed extensively in the biographies.
Regarding the term "narrative" (*shu*), the *Liji* states: "As for those who have no cause for sorrow, it must be King Wen alone;
he had Wang Ji as his father and King Wu as his son. His father established his position, and his son continued his work. It further says: "Zhongni (Confucius) followed the legacy of Yao..."

Shun followed the statutes and models of Wen and Wu; above, he conformed to the seasons of Heaven; below, he succeeded to the patterns of the earth and water. Now, I, the Chief of the Wise, dare not innovate, but merely follow and transmit his legacy.
Now, the second part [of this section] consists of three sections that correctly explain the main text. First, regarding the basis: "The Tathāgata is established as the definitive school.
Guishan says: "The Lord of the One Vehicle is the ten bodies. "The Ocean" refers to the samādhi upon which the present sutra relies. As the text below states:
"The teaching of the One Vehicle arises necessarily from within the Buddha’s Ocean-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi); it is not like the Three Vehicles and others, which rely on [other bases]."

Because the Buddha’s posterior-acquired wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) emerges [therefrom], it is designated as the "Ocean Seal" (*sāgaramudrā*). Qingliang said: "The Ocean Seal is a metaphor; it receives its name from this metaphor.

This means that when the fragrant ocean is clear and still, profoundly unmoving, the forms and images of all beings within the four continents appear therein, bearing seal-impressions (*mudrā*) just as a seal stamps an object.
It is also like ten thousand *qīng* of clear waves under a cloudless autumn sky. [The text continues with] "arranged..."
The stars and moon appear together in brilliant clarity; they neither come nor go, neither exist nor do not exist, neither one nor different.
In the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the waves of consciousness do not arise; it is limpid, pure, supremely luminous, and supremely still. Without thought, all things manifest instantaneously.
The mental inclinations, faculties, and desires of all sentient beings are present within this wisdom, like images reflected in the sea. Therefore—
The Sutra below states: "Just as the ocean universally manifests the bodies of sentient beings, it is for this reason called the great ocean.
Bodhi universally reflects all mental activities; therefore, Perfect Enlightenment is named 'Immeasurable.

It is not only that wisdom manifests in its entirety, but also that based on this wisdom, ten thousand forms are suddenly manifested to universally respond to all classes of beings. The *Bhadrapāla-parivarta* says: "Or manifesting the forms of boys or girls, [or] devas..."
Nāgas and asuras, up to mahoragas and so forth—each according to their inclinations, all are made to see them.
The forms and sizes of sentient beings are each different; their karmic actions and voices are likewise immeasurable.

All such things can be manifested through the majestic spiritual power of the Sāgaramudrā-samādhi, as explained at length in the *Xianshou-pin shu* (Commentary on the "Chapter on the Wise Leader"). Question: In the "Chapter on the Wise Leader," there is...
Regarding the ten kinds of samādhi, why do they rely solely on the Ocean-Seal (Sāgaramudrā)? The answer is: because from the very first, there is nothing that is not subsumed within them.
Thus, the *Dilun* states: "Within all that is taught in the ten phrases, there are always six kinds of gates of differentiated characteristics.

Furthermore, the "Appearance" chapter concerns the Buddha’s bodhi, while the "Worthy Head" chapter concerns Samantabhadra and others. Therefore, the *Tanxuanji* says: "The Ocean-Seal has two aspects: first, in terms of..."

Regarding the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*): as previously distinguished, the inexhaustible teachings all appear simultaneously, vividly, perfectly, and clearly within the Tathāgata’s Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgara-mudrā-samādhi*).
Second, regarding the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*): it is only through great Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra that one attains this samādhi and so forth.

The commentary states: although cause and fruit differ, their virtuous functions are similar, as explained in the *Xianshou pin shu* (Commentary on the "Chapter on the Excellence of the Head") which reconciles the illusory [nature of phenomena].
Regarding the analogy of space: that [preceding section] concerns the practice of the fruit, while this concerns the virtues of the cause.

Nevertheless, because the practices and virtues of Samantabhadra resemble the fruit of Buddhahood, both are measured by the extent of empty space. This is consistently stated throughout the preceding and following passages; reflect upon this.

However, although the ritual procedures differ, there is never any discrepancy in their essential meaning. As for *samādhi*, the *Tanyuan* (Probing the Profundities) states: it is "equal holding" (*samāhita*), because it is free from sinking and agitation.

Because concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are balanced, it is called "equanimity" (*samatā*). Because the mind is not distracted and dwells upon a single object, it is called "retention" (*dhāraṇā*).
To take the Dharma into the mind is termed "right reception" (*samyag-samādhi*).

To say that they "should be identical to the ocean of fruition" means there is an identity between the subject and object; yet cause and effect are not one. If one says they "should be identical," then cause and effect are not different.
Being neither one nor different constitutes the wisdom of the true ground. Reflect upon this.
The second [point] concerns the greatness of the two lower teachings. The *Neizhang* states: "There are three kinds of greatness in the teachings. Qingliang says:

First is the greatness of the accomplishment of the cause, which refers to the power of compassion and vows as the foundation for initiating practice; therefore, it is called the cause. Second is the greatness of the gradual accomplishment of the cause.

This refers to the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*), which serve as the causes for supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*). Because their arising is not instantaneous, they are called "gradual" (*krama*).

Third, "teaching and exposition" (*deśanā*) refers to the accomplishment of great cultivation; that is, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*). True cultivation accords with reality, and like direct realization, it can be expressed through verbal designations;

therefore, it is called "teaching and exposition. The two characters "teaching and exposition" specifically distinguish this from "great meaning," which—unlike the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*)—cannot be described.

Therefore, the first two do not resemble direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). Their essence is not profound or subtle; they do not require verbal discrimination, but serve merely as causes for supramundane wisdom.
Thus, they are both termed "causes. When their respective stages are attained, all three are accomplished. As for where these three stages are situated, there are two perspectives.

First, regarding the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), the first two may be included within the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmipūrva*), as they constitute the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for those grounds.

The latter one resides solely upon the ground (*bhūmi*). The second is explained in terms of general application. Within each ground, the cultivation of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and so forth, as well as the power of compassion and vows, constitute the accomplishment of the cause.

The wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*), etc., constitute the gradual progression of the cause. Both the fundamental realization (*mūla-adhigama*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) are taught as cultivation.

Regarding the "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and so forth, Taiyi said: "That which is called the 'cause' refers to the cultivation of skillful means and conditions; its essence is exhaustive."
The fulfillment of the stages refers precisely to Samantabhadra.
Regarding these two [stages], the following two demonstrate their mutual fusion; the *Commentary on the Grounds* states: (This is also an account by Xianshou. Third, concerning their mutual fusion:

within each of the aforementioned six [aspects], that which is "identity" (*ji*) is itself non-discourse, and non-discourse is itself discourse; both are fused without duality. This may be understood through reflection. Furthermore, as for the fruit...

1. Because the ocean is free from conditions (*pratyaya*), it cannot be described; that which is realized in relation to conditions can be described. 2. Because the two types of realization are not cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they cannot be described;
because the realizing subject arises through cultivation, it can be described. 3. Because correct realization is free from signs (*nimitta*), it cannot be described;

subsequent realization (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) carries signs, and thus it can be described. 4. Because subsequent realization is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), it cannot be described; [through] application...

When there is mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) in practice, it can be described. However, because the five preparatory contemplations (*prayoga-vipaśyanā*) are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), they cannot be described.

One may resort to dharmas to metaphorically indicate the stages (*bhūmi*); thus, they can be described. That which is above this cannot be described; yet, in each case, that which is indescribable is not different from that which is describable, because the ultimate truth (*tattva*) is all-pervasive.
That which is describable is not different from that which is indescribable, because the cultivation based on conditions has no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Therefore:
Although the following text explains only one portion, its meaning is nonetheless not slight; thus the treatise says: "Because it is grasped in suchness and in full. [The] commentary states:
The three [sections] are designated by the same name as this lower section; the meaning and intent of the upper and lower sections are the same.
Regarding the two sections on the universal [practice]: first, the classification of the gates. As for "Universal" (Samantabhadra), Taiyi said:
"Although it begins with Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī), its perfection lies in being all-pervasive; therefore, Mañjuśrī is hidden, and only Samantabhadra is mentioned. Ketang said:
"As for the differentiation of characteristics, expedient means have no substance and are entirely empty; when one thoroughly investigates the True Vehicle, one sits [in realization]."
The Dharma-realm is severed. If it were to encompass [all things], then the three vehicles would have no basis. It is accomplished through the Universal Dharma (pu-fa). The old [translation] says:
"Perfect fusion means there is no such thing as the Universal Dharma. Form is itself emptiness; within emptiness there is no form. Three is itself one; within the one there is no three.
Therefore it is said that the three vehicles must ultimately come to an end. If this is so, then all other vehicles are exhausted, leaving only the One Vehicle (ekayāna). How can this be?
In the interim, other matters are accommodated. Therefore, these two gates together elucidate distinct tenets.

Regarding the "Gate of Distinguishing Characteristics" (*bun-sō-mon*) and the following two gates, there are two sections for their sequential explanation. First, within the Gate of Distinguishing Characteristics, there are four parts. The first is the differentiation of the provisional and the real according to their respective schools. As for the Gate of Distinguishing Characteristics:

it is the analytical discernment of the differences between the characteristics of the three and the one teachings. As the text below states: "Precisely because of this Dharma, it is difficult to transcend the realm of ordinary sentiment."
Faith. Therefore, the Sage takes those three vehicles and contrasts them with the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Regarding what distinguishes it from the three vehicles, Taiyi says: "The distinct teaching is distinct from the three vehicles. Qingliang says: "The latter one directly reveals the fundamental Dharma and is consistently non-common (*asādhāraṇa*).
He further states: "Only the latter one is the non-common One Vehicle. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* points to this.

It is "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other such scriptures are taught in common with the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Furthermore, it is said: "The 'distinct' is precisely the unshared, for it is sudden, real, and unique.
Again, it is said: "It is not shared with the two vehicles; however, regarding the 'one' and the 'three,' there are two theories within the five teachings (*pañca-deśanā*).

One theory holds that the preceding teachings constitute the three vehicles, while the final one constitutes the one vehicle (*ekayāna*), as briefly cited previously. For details, see the *Kongō-kyō* (Vajracchedikā).

The *Mumen Dando Tamgen Zashō* (Miscellaneous Chapters on Investigating the Profundity through Questions and Answers) states that the initial "Small" [Vehicle] constitutes the Three Vehicles, while the latter three constitute the One Vehicle, as is fully detailed in the *Huayan jing shu* (Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra), the *Yuanjue jing shu* (Commentary on the Complete Enlightenment Sutra), and other works. The reason for this is that the final and sudden teachings differ in their respective approaches to progression and regression.

If categorized according to all being for three types of persons, then the middle three constitute three [teachings]. If categorized according to the sublation of duality, which differs from the former, then the latter three are all one.
Thus, the *Taiyi* says: "If the subsequent [teachings] refute attachments to establish the correct principle, they belong to the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*).

This includes the view that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, as well as the fourfold Buddha-nature of the Mahāyāna *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. These are not [the views of] the Hīnayāna or those who have turned back [from the Great Vehicle]."
The "mind-person" refers to the Buddha-nature and the Great Parinirvāṇa according to the Sudden Teaching and the Final Teaching.

From this point onward, it is also taught that the latter three [teachings] are unified as one, while the former two are differentiated as three. This present chapter primarily employs the former explanation to establish the formal structure of the text;
this can be seen through careful reflection.

The following two sections are established as authoritative by means of scriptural citations. Regarding the phrase "such as the Lotus Sūtra," Taoyi states that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of seeking a separate "great ox-cart" outside the three realms.

However, regarding these three subsequent sections on the manifestation of the Sage’s words, first is the formal indication. Question: From the perspective of the *Jiāngjiā* (Chapter on the Master), how does it compare to the *Zhìxiāng* (Chapter on the Ultimate Reality)?
Answer: The ten meanings are differentiated, yet from beginning to end they are equally harmonious; such is the natural order of principle. Why, then, should one offer criticism or reproach?
How much more so for one who has condensed this chapter, achieving abundance of meaning with brevity of expression?

Furthermore, in the case of the *Awakening of Faith*, the root text does not exceed a single fascicle, yet the commentary fills an entire volume; how could this be considered a matter of gain or loss? The *Xiaochao* asks:
"As for the difference between the Mahāyāna and the One Vehicle, many scholars of the Faxiang school do not believe in it; therefore, Master Huayan Zang..."

In the *Wujiaoyi fenqi wen* (Treatise on the Delimitation of the Meanings of the Five Teachings), the distinctions between the ten meanings of the Mahāyāna and the One Vehicle are analyzed and distinguished, with more than twenty sutras and śāstras cited as evidence.
Thus, one should know that those whose learning and understanding are shallow and limited cannot avoid slandering the Dharma;

how could this be otherwise? Answer: In literary composition, the underlying intent is primary. Only by "reaching back to the intent" through the words can one truly grasp it. Why is this so? Furthermore, regarding this...

In his commentary on the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, [Zhi]yi comprehensively distinguishes [the teachings] from the preceding four; in his sub-commentary on the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, Fazang alone disparages the three provisional vehicles.

How could one rashly take Guishan’s citation of them at a single moment to establish their replacement, or measure Xianshou’s assessment across a millennium? Otherwise, consider Guangzhai’s "four vehicles":
would the fact that our Patriarch cited them as the reality of that past era mean they were no different from the reality of today? No, it would not.

Consider this carefully. First, the provisional; second, the correct explanation of the ten [categories]. First, the distinction between the provisional and the real, in three parts. Initially, citing a metaphor to clarify the provisional and the real, in three parts.

First, the direct manifestation of their characteristics. Regarding the "provisional and real": this is explained in terms of ultimate skillful means (*upāya*). As for "skillful means," it refers to that which is provisionally bestowed.

Furthermore, among the five teachings, the last one is ultimate while the preceding four are provisional (*upāya*). Question: Since the names "Final" and "Sudden" refer to the actual, why are they considered provisional? Answer:
Although the two teachings—the Third and Fourth—eliminate duality and differ from the former [teachings], they manifest the One by contrast with the Three;

because they employ skillful means to accord with the capacities of sentient beings, they are also called provisional teachings. Question: The *Great Sutra Commentary* (Dajing shu), in its account of Guangzhai, states: "If one relies on the past, it was not yet revealed..."

[The opponent] says: "If it is taught that all possess the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and that those whose seeds were destroyed are now all declared to have attained Buddhahood, then there is a discrepancy between the former and the latter teachings.
How can these be reconciled? [The respondent] answers: "Simply understand that text, and you will know for yourself the vast difference between them. Guishan said:
"Prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, there was also a 'single reality,' which refers to the sudden teaching of the Tathāgata-garbha as true and eternal for a certain class of those with sharp faculties."

This is the principle. Furthermore, various *prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and works such as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* all implicitly rely on the ultimate truth (*tattva*) to censure the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna*).

However, because the capacities and understandings of those who hear them differ, these texts do not concurrently present the provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*). Thus, Kāśyapa reproached himself, saying:

"For example, just as a man whose sense organs are ruined can no longer derive benefit from the five desires, so too a śrāvaka whose fetters are severed [can no longer benefit others] regarding the Buddha..."

Within the Dharma, there is no further benefit [for them]. [They know for themselves that they will not attain Buddhahood. It is also said: "Why have we forever severed our roots? Regarding this Mahāyāna, we are like spoiled seeds.
This reveals that their afflictions (*kleśa*) have already been severed and can no longer sprout.

Now, the three classes of *śrāvaka* disciples in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are all granted predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Those *śrāvakas* who are not present in this assembly are commanded to propagate and expound [the teaching].

All sentient beings are my children. Opening up the provisional and harmonizing with the provisional, there is only this single reality. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is called "wondrous" (*miau*); the wondrousness lies precisely here.

However, the reality to which one returns is none other than the reality of the past; it is simply because that past reality was not yet harmonized with the present that it is now considered "wondrous.
Furthermore, even Guangzhai did not explicitly reveal that the One Vehicle reality existed of itself from the very beginning.

[This is] the teaching. (In the *Lotus Sūtra*, only the former provisional [teachings] are reconciled; the former reality is not reconciled. This is because the former reality does not remain stuck in expedient means.

Yet, to claim that only the *Lotus Sūtra* teaches the reality [of the One Vehicle] would suppress all other Mahāyāna sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This is a deficiency. The doctrine of the four vehicles is well-established through both scripture and reason.

The commentary states: Since Mount Gui did not reconcile the reality, how could it be only Qingliang who reconciled it? It was solely due to Guangzhai that both [the provisional and the real] were [treated as such]. The former...

Because the sutra belongs to the provisional and belongs to the comprehensive synthesis (*hui*), Qingliang specifically set forth several categories to refute it. Now, you instead claim that Qingliang’s categories comprehensively synthesize the former reality;
how can this be such extreme ignorance? If you say that Guangzhai did not distinguish the former reality but blended it all into one, thereby creating the contradiction, [then consider this:
Qingliang did distinguish the former reality, and only thereafter, based on the actual substance, did he... [not]... [blend it].

They are all equally included within the assembly; thus, that which constitutes their convergence is such that, although there was a distinction between the provisional and the real in the past—whether they were differentiated or not—they are nonetheless equal in being a convergence.
This is precisely like "fifty paces laughing at a hundred paces": though the distances differ, both are equally instances of running.
Why must it be that only Qingliang is correct while Guangzhai is not? If Guangzhai says, "I am precisely..."
Because the substantial reality is insufficient, [the provisional] is entirely negated as being merely expedient; thus, all are ultimately unified.

Therefore, Qingliang’s refutation merely indulges in voluminous rhetoric—substituting one swallow for another. How could it achieve anything? Could it be that Qingliang was such a partisan who acted in this manner? Question:

Why does the *Chao* (Commentary) state that regarding the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles, the former is provisional while the latter is real, yet that because the substantial reality is insufficient, they all belong to...?

Is it like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other [sutras]? The answer is: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* merely brings together the provisional teachings of the past and returns them to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the present;

it does not bring together the reality of the past. Since the reality of the past is fundamentally the One Vehicle, there is no need to bring it together with this [present] essence, as the essence of consciousness is not transformed when consciousness is transformed into wisdom.
The essence of consciousness is fundamentally pure, for it is the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*). How wondrous is this principle!

Who can truly know this? To state the essential point: one may simply regard the Initial Teaching (Shijiao) of our own school as provisional (*upāya*) and the latter three teachings as real (*tattva*).

These are then correlated with the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), such that the former is provisional and the latter is real. Thus, Zhenguō said: "The *Lotus Sūtra* states: 'The teaching for the śrāvakas has been definitively resolved;
the remaining assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise be so. Furthermore, it says: 'There are two ways of citing the *Lotus Sūtra'."
The text serves as proof for the principle that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures will all attain Buddhahood. First is the "Dharma Master" chapter:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know: such persons as these, if they have not heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, remain very far from the Buddha’s wisdom.

If they hear this profound sūtra—which definitively resolves the Dharma of the Śrāvakas and is the king of all sūtras—and having heard it, contemplate it with earnest attention, you should know that such a person..."

"...and so forth. They are close to the Buddha's wisdom. The commentary states: Since it is said that they have definitively realized the Śrāvaka-dharma, this clarifies that the Śrāvakas of former times—such as those mentioned in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and other texts—are like men whose sense organs are ruined;
regarding the five desires, they can no longer derive benefit from them. Furthermore, they are like scorched grain sprouts.

As stated in the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*, they are like scorched grain sprouts: even if they encounter the spring sunshine, there is no hope for an autumn harvest. And as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*: [they are like...]
...and so forth. It was said that those of fixed nature could not attain Buddhahood, yet the minds of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles were all filled with hesitation;

now, it is revealed that they shall all become Buddhas, and thus it is called "the definitive resolution, foremost. The Sūtra says: "When the Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed;
the twelve hundred Arhats shall likewise all become Buddhas. Therefore, it is called "definitive resolution. Furthermore, fearing that people might say, "The twelve hundred..."

Externally, those śrāvakas of fixed nature will not become buddhas; therefore, the subsequent passage is cited from the beginning of the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Predictions," where all one thousand two hundred disciples seek their predictions. The Tathāgata first bestows the prediction upon Cunda to become a buddha, followed by the five hundred.
The final verse says: "Those five hundred bhikṣus shall successively become buddhas, all bearing the same name, 'Universal' (Samantabhadra)."
[The Buddha] spoke clearly, bestowing the prophecy in successive order: "After my parinirvāṇa, such-and-such a person shall become a Buddha.

The world he shall transform shall be just like mine today; the majesty and purity of his land, as well as his supernormal powers, his assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, his True Dharma and Semblance Dharma, and the duration of his lifespan in kalpas—all shall be exactly as described above. Kāśyapa, you have already..."
"Know this: the five hundred masters and the rest of the assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise be so. For those who are not present in this assembly, you should proclaim it for them.
The commentary states: Based on this, it is not merely that twelve hundred are enumerated; rather, the assembly at Vulture Peak consisted of twelve thousand people.
The five thousand who rose from their seats were practitioners of overweening pride (*adhimāna*); they must have been śrāvakas who were not included among those at Vulture Peak.

Regarding the "Excellence of the Lotus Assembly on Mount [Xiangshan]," it causes the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas within this assembly to receive their respective predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

The rest is as explained in the *Xuánzōng*. Furthermore, one may also subsume those four vehicles under the two teachings of the beginning and the end (though one must exclude the former "Real" Dharma Lotus which did not convene such an assembly).

Zhenguó said: "Indeed, at the conclusion of the gradual teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*, as it was about to gather in those who had failed, it further caused them to depart, thereby exhorting those present in the assembly."

This causes them to believe and accept it. This sutra marks the beginning of the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*). To manifest its profound superiority, [the Buddha] withheld it from being heard, so that later students might cultivate the seeds of seeing and hearing it.
Furthermore, it says: "Now, regarding the *Lotus Sutra*," below which he explains and reconciles two sutras; this is based on the ritual of transformation (*hua-yi*).

Regarding the two teachings of gradual and sudden, they collectively explain the intent of the sūtras. As for the *Lotus Sūtra* being "gradual," it is because the method of conversion (*huayi*) is gradual:

first, the three vehicles are taught to guide sentient beings, and only thereafter are they delivered and liberated solely by means of the Great Vehicle; hence it is called "gradual. It does not mean that the dharma-gate itself is gradual.
As for the phrase "about to gather in those of ruined seeds," the meaning is as previously cited: it refers to those of the two vehicles whose fetters have been severed.
A man whose faculties are ruined finds no benefit in the five desires; he is like a parched grain seed that cannot produce a sprout. This was the intent of the former teachings.
Now, having reached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the three classes of śrāvakas all receive their predictions of enlightenment. Even those not present in this assembly shall be proclaimed [to attain it].
Thus, parched grain produces sprouts, the blind dragon regains its hearing, the corpse rises again, and cold ashes grow warm—saying that the harvest is near.
This has not yet been explained in detail; first, let us put it into practice so that those gathered here may personally rejoice in their great fortune.
Therefore, it is said: "Be earnest and diligent. For this reason, the Sūtra states: "This assembly is without branches and leaves;

there are only the pure and solid. The commentary says: "Since the profuse twigs have perished, the solid trunk remains. Only after the detailed explanation is given will one then gather [the essence]; thus, even those not present in the assembly [will benefit].
Please explain this for me. To say that this sutra is the beginning of the sudden teaching (*tongo*) means that it was first established as a sudden exposition;

therefore, there is no lingering attachment to expedient means (*upāya*), nor is there any need to lead [beings] through gradual practice. It directly reveals what is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), manifesting the inconceivable Dharma. Those present in the assembly did not hear it because they lacked the causal seeds.
If one cultivates the seeds of causes, what is there that one would not hear? Therefore, it is said: "To cause the cultivation of the seeds of seeing and hearing. The critique states:
Even if one does not believe that Guishan, then this Qingliang may still be trusted. Do not harbor baseless attachments.
Thus, could there be any fault in Kang’s alternating between censure and approval? It is said: "The gentleman of antiquity, upon erring, would correct himself; the gentleman of today, upon erring..."
This is to accord with it. Question: Does this mean that merely understanding the three provisional vehicles as such is sufficient? Answer:

To comprehensively understand the three vehicles in terms of both the provisional and the real is the great principle of our school; it was not something attained by Dharma Master Guangzhai. As will be explained in the text below. Question:

In this context, do the sheep and deer represent those of dull capacity (*mṛdu-dharmaka*) or those who penetrate the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*)? Answer: There are three explanations regarding this. First, some say they are of dull capacity. Second, some say...

whereas the *Wúliàngyì jīng* (Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings) states they have severed them and have moved, and thus they are not of the "Dull-Witted Dharma" (*yūhō*). As for the "four crossroads," the *Jiàocháo* states they refer to the Four Noble Truths.
Below "The Great White [Vehicle]," Zhenyuan says: "The 'Great Vehicle' (mahāyāna) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom.

Regarding the following two lines, they exclude divergent interpretations. An ancient objection states: 'In the verses of the "Expedient Means" chapter, it is described that the past teaching of the Small [Vehicle] was an expedient means, but it is not described that the Great [Vehicle] was an expedient means.
One should know that for the Sons of the Buddha, the Mahāyāna is not an expedient means; why then is there suddenly [a claim otherwise]? "
In the fifth section of the *Wenju* (Textual Explanations), he replies: "Have you not heard that in the 'Chapter on Lifespan' (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*), it says:
'When I was young and left home, I attained *sambodhi*. Everything from that point until now—whether small or great, whether my own or another's—is all my skillful means (*upāya*).

The same is true for all Buddhas. How could one not seek [the truth]? Nor is it inferior. Furthermore, an ancient critic objects: "The two [aspects] are skillful means and may thus be called 'seeking'."
The text states: "Only this one reality is true; the other two are not real. Inferring from this, it appears that while one [aspect] is sought, the other two are not. Yet he further replies:

The 'one' that previously depended upon the two has phenomena existing outside of it. Thus, while the name is the same, the essence differs. This is a dark adherence to the 'tile and spark' or the 'fish.'"
"Eye" refers to the moon’s form at night, shining with light. The ignorant are foolish, while the wise feel compassion for them;
therefore, the following three sections present the original text of the sutra. The commentary states: "Seeking" has three meanings:

first, the sense of a great capacity [of the practitioner] evoking a fruit, wherein seeking is discussed within that capacity; second, the secret pursuit within one's emotions as to whether the goal will be attained or not; third, the verbal act of seeking.
This refers precisely to the three earnest entreaties. Within the teachings of the past, there were already two requests, though they had not yet been voiced.

Reaching the present day, these three solicitations are complete. If one asks whether the three requests made when formerly leaving the household were requests arising from the disposition of the faculties (*indriya*), the text states:
As previously promised, this involves seeking three; why then is there a deficiency in seeking one? The answer is: having gone outside and not seeing [the third], there must be some other path.
One takes what was previously promised as three to seek a different meaning, yet this is also tantamount to seeking one.
In this context, the lower two [vehicles] are combined to clarify the seeking of the fruit. The text states:

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, "This vehicle departs from the triple world and dwells within *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). If one has already mounted this vehicle even before departing, why would one struggle to leave the burning house?
For what reason, then, is it further said that "the chariots are outside the gate"? If they were already outside, by what means would one depart? However, the term "vehicle" (*yāna*) is pervasive.

Regarding cause and effect: the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*) that sever the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are all the causal vehicle (*hetu-yāna*).

The knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and non-arising (*kṣaya-anutpāda-jñāna*) is all termed the resultant vehicle (*phala-yāna*). One must rely on the causal vehicle to sever and exhaust all delusions before one can attain the resultant vehicle’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and non-arising;

therefore, it is said that "the carriage is outside the gate. This refers to the result as the primary factor and the cause as secondary; speaking from the perspective of the result, the carriage is outside the gate. If [discussing] the internal cause...

The severing of fetters is what constitutes the movement; thus, "vehicle" (*yāna*) is defined by the sense of movement. External fruits do not involve such movement, so how could they be called vehicles?

However, while these fruits lack the movement of severing afflictions, it is only through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) that one enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which alone constitutes a true movement.

Question: Regarding the two [lower] and three [higher] vehicles, the inquiry is posed to provide an explanation of the four. The first two concern whether the vehicles have a fruit or not; the inquiry asks:
"If one reaches the fruit by means of the vehicle's cause, for what reason does one subsequently seek a cart?"
Answer: Based on the two or three lower vehicles, there is nothing to be attained; thus, one should provide two responses. First, establishing the principle to answer:

(1) Citing the sūtra as the formal response. The Mahāyāna is itself the One Vehicle. If viewed from the perspective of the two lower vehicles, it is distinguished according to their respective tenets.
Therefore, the sūtra below says: "He gives each of them [what they need]; it is not appropriate to differentiate. The *Wenju* says: "Without shifting their original habits, he reveals [the truth]."

This is true. For example, Śāriputra opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through wisdom, while Maudgalyāyana opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and so forth.
This is intended to turn back the minds of those below [the two vehicles] by extending [the teaching]. First, the actual demonstration: the text states that the present passage contains the request.
Together with Ānanda, among those who heard the Dharma were twelve hundred people, headed by Śāriputra, who made a fervent triple request.
Among the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Maitreya was the leader; these sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth numbered eighty thousand in total.

With palms joined in a reverent heart, they desired to hear the complete path. At the beginning of the parables, Śāriputra requested on behalf of those of middling faculties, and furthermore, for all [beings].

The "Request by the Fourfold Assembly" serves as the request for those of inferior capacity. The text says: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly.
The "Permission Granted by Dharma" says: "Since you have earnestly requested three times, how could I not speak?

The "Permission Granted by Parable" says: "I shall further clarify this meaning through a parable. The "Permission Granted by Causes and Conditions" says: "The causes and conditions of my past lives and yours..."
Now it shall be explained. The explanation of the Dharma being concluded, Śāriputra rejoiced. The explanation by way of parables being concluded, Kāśyapa and the others rejoiced.
The explanation of past lives being concluded, Rāhula rejoiced. Furthermore, the combined text of the parables states:

"To cause all these sons to constantly engage in play day and night for kalpas, and together with the bodhisattvas, to ride upon this precious vehicle straight to the site of enlightenment. Therefore, it says, "For the sake of desiring," and so forth.
Furthermore, if one does not establish two criteria for certainty, there is an ancient objection which says: "If a bodhisattva were to seek [the teaching], the bodhisattvas would have understood it;

since there is no such understanding, we know they did not seek it. The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) replies: "Have you not heard that when the Dharma exposition was concluded, the fourfold assembly of devas, nāgas, and others all attained understanding?
As for those who are not bodhisattvas, what do you think they are? This continues down to the third point, where the sutra provides the definitive conclusion.

It is said: Just as that elder, seeing his children safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place of fearlessness, considered his own wealth to be immeasurable and bestowed great chariots equally upon all his children.
Question: Regarding "descending below," the third section asks about the reality and unreality of the three vehicles as revealed by the "three times.
Answer: Truly descending below; the fourth section answers that both meanings of "expedient means" (upāya) are universally applicable.

Guishan said: "The cause is the same while the principle (zong) differs; this meaning is truly profound. However, the *Wenju* states: "Now, for more than forty years, the Buddha has been with the world, and only now does he reveal the Truth."
This is indeed so. As for the citations provided above, they employ that text to establish this meaning; it is the height of subtlety. Regarding the distinction between the two teachings:
"teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the cause, and "meaning" (*yi*) refers to the fruit. Because cause and fruit differ, they are said to be distinct.

This section has three parts; first, the formal clarification. The subsequent text states: "Alternatively, both teaching and meaning are taught, when viewed from the perspective of the Three Vehicles..."
Because of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Alternatively, it refers to both the teaching and its meaning, as the One Vehicle is contrasted with the Three Vehicles.
Therefore, the two citations below serve as proof; nor do the three [points] below refute error, for they are likewise unattainable for both vehicles.

Regarding this, the *Yanyi* (Exposition of the Meaning) states: "The sheep and deer carts are merely empty pointers. If one has already left the gate, one does not board a carriage. If the ox cart were real, then upon leaving..."

The gate was immediately closed, and even the ox-cart could not pass through. This clarifies that all three were merely provisional pointers. Speaking in terms of the Dharma, the former [teachings] pointed to the three vehicles:
outside the gates of the triple world, the two vehicles exit the triple world but possess no true realization; whereas the Bodhisattva exits the realm.
How could there be any true realization? Since both lack true realization, they are called "not ascending the chariot.
It is clearly known that the three vehicles are all provisional establishments (seeking the meaning through the teaching—that is, the two measures of teaching and principle).

Regarding the fourfold distinction of what was originally sought: first is the explicit explanation; the text states: "Originally one sought the sheep, the deer, and the water buffalo, hoping to transcend the stage of segmented birth (*paricchinna-bhava*).
Now, having obtained the white ox, one exhausts the stage of transformation (*pariṇāmi-bhava*), surpassing what was originally hoped for;
how could one not rejoice? Second is the citation of scriptural evidence; third is the refutation of errors; and finally, fourth, is the conclusion.

The second part, "The Distinctions in the Measurement of the Four Virtues," has two sections. The first, "The Common Teaching," has two parts. First, the indication of the characteristics: this refers to the Mahāyāna within the lower three [vehicles] and the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) revealed below.
Furthermore, the subsequent sections may be understood by analogy. The concluding reference to these points below is as stated in the *Gufu-ki*: [The text continues with the specific citations.]

This is because the analogy of the ocean water is the same, which explains why it cannot be termed a "same teaching. Now, the commentary states: "Same..."

The teachings are fivefold: the first is called the Elementary Teaching; the second, the Initial Teaching; the third, the Final Teaching; the fourth, the Sudden Teaching;

and the fifth, the Perfect Teaching. Whether expanded or condensed, these possess both distinctions and commonalities. They harmonize the perfect mind of true enlightenment and transform the heterodox views of the future.
They eternally provide a standard for reflection and truly sharpen the "ox-knife" of the Dharma. Those who follow this learning are as numerous as clouds, beyond all counting.

opening and closing. First, the indication: "1. Alternatively," etc., which opens and explains five points. First, the unification. The *Great Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "First, they are collectively treated as one.

However, as all [the preceding teachings] provide access for those entering via the three vehicles, they are called "teachings of the three vehicles. The latter [teaching], on the other hand, directly reveals the fundamental Dharma and does not accommodate the two vehicles;

It is called "common" because it enables those of the three vehicles to equally contemplate and thereby derive benefit; thus, it carries the meaning of the "three vehicles.
